 IN THE MATTER OF SOUTHWESTERN                                           §

                       OCCIDENTAL PERMIAN LTD.’S EXCEPTIONS TO
                        PROPOSED CERTIFICATION OF STIPULATION

I.     INTRODUCTION

       Occidental Permian Ltd. (“OPL”) was a signatory to the Comprehensive Stipulation filed

on June 22, 2026 (the “Stipulation”), which was the product of extensive negotiations and

compromise between Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) and every party that

represents the interests of SPS’s customers, with the exception of NMPRC Staff. OPL appreciates

the Hearings Examiners’ thorough review of the Stipulation and agrees with their overall

conclusion that the Stipulation was the product of serious bargaining among capable,

knowledgeable parties and, as a whole, produces fair, just, and reasonable rates. 1 However, OPL

urges the Commission to reject the Hearings Examiners’ proposed modifications to the Stipulation,

which would result in a final order that would deviate substantially from the parties’ carefully

negotiated bargain. Instead, the Commission should approve and adopt the Stipulation in all

respects, without modification.




       1
           Certification of Stipulation (“Certification”) at 150, 153.

                                                           1
         In particular, OPL takes exception to two of the Hearings Examiners’ proposed

modifications to Section 1.11 (Revenue Allocation and Rate Design):

        •     Finding (9)(e)(i), to the extent it rejects the Stipulation’s use of SPS’s annual single
              coincident peak (“1CP) to calculate the system load factor in the Average and Excess
              Demand – Four Coincident Peak (“AED-4CP”) allocation methodology, and
              recommends using a four-coincident-peak (“4CP”) load factor instead. 2
        •     Finding (9)(e)(iii), which rejects the Stipulation’s allocation of production tax credits
              (“PTCs”) on an energy (Energy-at-Source) basis and instead recommends that PTCs
              be allocated using the AED-4CP allocator. 3
        Neither modification is necessary to produce fair, just, and reasonable rates. The stipulated

1CP load factor matches the textbook method for applying the AED-4CP method from the

NARUC Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manual (“NARUC CAM”), mirrors SPS’s own practice

in Texas, and was referred to as the “industry standard” method by SPS’s witnesses. The stipulated

energy allocation of PTCs matches the way PTCs are created—per kilowatt-hour generated—and

the way SPS already allocates the Hale and Sagamore wind PTCs through its energy-based Fuel

and Purchased Power Cost Adjustment Clause (“FPPCAC”). The Commission should approve

Section 1.11 as stipulated.

II.     STANDARD OF REVIEW

        The Commission has a long-standing policy of encouraging settlements and evaluates a

contested stipulation by asking whether it is the product of serious bargaining, whether as a whole

it benefits customers and the public interest, and whether as a whole it violates any important

regulatory principle or practice. 4 The Commission adjudicates the specific terms in dispute, but

“its ultimate approval finding concerns the lawfulness and reasonableness of the stipulation as a

 whole.” 5 Importantly, the Stipulation’s provisions are “interdependent and not severable,” and

Section 1.11’s class allocation terms were reached “through compromise of the issues raised in

this case.” 6 A modification to one negotiated term of that compromise should therefore rest on a

record showing that the stipulated term is itself unreasonable—not merely that another approach

could also be defended. As shown below, the record does not support either of the proposed

modifications to Section 11.1 of the Stipulation.

III.   EXCEPTIONS

       A.         Exception No. 1 (Certification Finding (9)(e)(i)): The Commission should
                  approve the stipulated 1CP system load factor in the AED-4CP class cost
                  allocation methodology.

                  1.        Background on the AED-4CP class allocation methodology.

       The AED-4CP allocation methodology explicitly considers both energy usage and peak

demand when developing class allocation factors. The AED-4CP allocation factors are derived

using the following formula:

                  AED = (AD% x SLF%) + [ED% x (1 – SLF%)]
                  Where:
                  AD% = A class’s share of Average Demand (or energy usage);
                  ED% = A class’s share of Excess Demand, which is the difference between a
                        class’s Peak Demand and its Average Demand; and
                  SLF% = System Load Factor, which is the ratio of the average load over a
                        designated period to the peak demand occurring in that period. 7
       The AED-4CP allocator weights each class’s share of average demand by the system load

factor, and each class’s share of excess demand by one minus the system load factor. 8 The AD

 component of AED is the product of each class’s percent of average demand (i.e., energy

consumption) and the system load factor. 9 This measures the amount of capacity costs that would

be incurred if the utility served the same size load at a constant 100% load factor. 10 The ED

component of AED measures the relative variability of each class’s load. 11 The greater a class’s

load variability, the greater the amount of load-following resources (e.g., simple-cycle and

combined-cycle gas turbines) needed to provide service. 12

                  2.       The Stipulation correctly uses SPS’s system 1CP to determine the
                           “system load factor” in the AED-4CP allocation, and adopting the
                           Stipulation would bring SPS into line with standard industry practice.

       The record clearly rebuts the Hearings Examiners’ finding that “there is not substantial

justification provided by the Signatories for the shift” to using SPS’s system 1CP to determine the

AED-4CP system load factor. 13 System load factor is defined as “the ratio of the average load

over a designated period to the peak demand occurring in that period.” 14 SPS’s application used

the average of four summer monthly peaks as the denominator, which, as OPL witness Ly

explained, “is not a proper definition of system load factor.” 15 Mr. Ly continued, “The only

appropriate way to apply AED-4CP is to weight average demand by the system annual or 1CP

load factor. The use of a 1CP load factor is consistent with the typical application of the AED

method. Further, the NARUC CAM states that the annual system peak load factor should be used

 in applying the AED method.” 16 At the hearing, Mr. Ly described the Stipulation’s use of the 1CP

to calculate the AED-4CP system load factor as “essentially just a standardization” that makes

SPS’s otherwise “nearly correct” calculation “comport with established practice.” 17 And SPS’s

witnesses agreed. SPS witness Hurt testified that “the 1-CP is the industry standard” and that

“[n]ot a lot of utilities, to my knowledge, use a 4-CP System Load Factor.” 18 SPS witness

Trowbridge testified that “in traditional Cost Allocation, the 1-CP method in an AED-4CP is more

common, and that’s presented in the NARUC manual,” and that the 1CP “gives a true measure of

excess, which is Capacity required above average usage,” because SPS remains “a Summer

peaking Utility” and “that single peak is what we must meet.” 19 Further, SPS has used its system

1CP to determine the AED-4CP system load factor in its Texas rate cases, where the Public Utility

Commission of Texas has consistently approved it. 20 Accordingly, contrary to the Hearings

Examiners’ finding, 21 the record clearly supports the use of SPS’s system 1CP to determine the

system load factor for the AED-4CP allocation.

                   3.       The Certification does not adequately justify departing from the
                            Stipulation and using SPS’s system 4CP as the system load factor.

        The Certification does not contain any persuasive justification for departing from the

Signatories’ agreement to use the 1CP to establish the AED-4CP system load factor. Rather than

any principled cost allocation arguments, the Hearings Examiners’ proposal to use a 4CP system

 load factor to calculate the AED-4CP appears to be driven primarily by the fact that using a 1CP

system load factor results in more costs being allocated to SPS’s Residential class. 22 While that

may be true, the Commission should keep in mind that the Stipulation was the product of extensive

bargaining between SPS and various stakeholder groups, and that other terms in the Stipulation

were sufficiently favorable to the Residential class that that class’s designated representative, the

NMDOJ, signed on to and supported the Stipulation.

       The Certification rests heavily on the fact that a 4CP load factor “has been the status quo

for a good period of time on SPS’s system.” 23 However Mr. Ly explained that OPL’s consultants

have repeatedly raised this issue in prior SPS rate cases, but because SPS’s recent rate cases settled,

“this issue has been punted down the line,” so that the 4CP weighting persisted as “a matter of

inertia.” 24 And SPS witness Mr. Hurt confirmed that this application used 4CP simply by

“following the status quo.” 25 But settled practice that has not been litigated on the merits is not

evidence that the practice is correct, and it is not a reason to override a negotiated correction that

every customer-representative Signatory accepted. This is especially true where, as discussed

above, there is ample evidence in the record to support using the 1CP, and no evidence upon which

the Commission could conclude that a 4CP load factor better reflects cost causation on SPS’s

system.

       The Hearings Examiners also note that in Case No. 25-00085-UT, the parties agreed to

engage in a series of stakeholder workshops to consider changes to SPS’s allocation

methodologies. However, the Stipulation in this proceeding does not impact that prior agreement

 in the slightest, and those workshops will still be held. The Certification notes that the “Stipulation

makes a decision to change an allocation method prior to Staff and other parties participating in

workshops that are intended to address the question of whether allocation changes are appropriate

given the shift from dispatchable to variable resources.” 26 But the fact that workshops will be held

in the future to consider alternative allocation methodologies does not mean that changes are

unjustified in the present, especially when those changes are broadly supported by SPS and its

customers. And as noted above, applying the 1CP system load factor in the AED-4CP calculation

is, simply, correct.       There is no reason to delay that correction simply because additional

methodological changes could occur in the future. Whatever alternative allocators the workshops

ultimately recommend, the question in this case is how to calculate the AED-4CP method the

Commission is approving now. On that question, the record evidence uniformly points to 1CP.

       B.         Exception No. 2 (Certification Finding (9)(e)(iii)): The Commission should
                  approve the stipulated “Energy-at-Source” allocation of PTCs.

                  1.       Allocating the value of PTCs based on each customer class’s energy
                           usage is fair to all of SPS’s customers and consistent with cost-causation
                           principles.

       The Commission should reject the Hearings Examiners’ proposal to depart from the

Stipulation by using AED-4CP rather than “Energy-at-Source” to allocate PTCs among SPS’s

customer classes because the record is clear that the “Energy-at-Source” allocator conforms with

cost causation principles and is fair to all of SPS’s customers. Section 1.11 of the Stipulation

provides that the value of the PTCs from SPS’s renewable generation will be allocated on an

energy basis, 27 meaning that SPS will flow the value of the PTCs it generates back to each




       26
            Certification at ¶ 156.
       27
            Signatories Ex. 1, Comprehensive Stipulation at 10, § 1.11.

                                                         7
 customer class in direct proportion to the amount of energy that SPS generates to serve that class. 28

This allocation methodology is fair and reasonable, and should be approved.

        The fundamental justification for allocating PTCs on an energy basis is straightforward:

PTCs are created in direct proportion to the energy generated by qualifying renewable generation

facilities. 29 The IRS calculates the PTC credit that SPS receives by “multiplying eligible kilowatt-

hours of electricity by the applicable credit rate,” so “[t]he amount of the credit therefore turns on

energy production, not retail revenue, or the price a customer pays.” 30 The Energy-at-Source

allocator starts with each class’s metered kWh, adjusts for the line losses incurred to serve each

voltage level, and allocates PTCs according to each class’s share of the resulting source energy,

so that “[e]ach class thus receives a share of the PTC value associated with the amount of electricity

SPS must generate to serve it.” 31 Accordingly, an energy allocation aligns with cost causation

principles because it maintains a direct, logical connection between how PTCs are created (by SPS

generating renewable kWh) and how the PTCs’ value is funneled back to customers (based on the

amount of renewable kWh the customer causes SPS to generate). Just as the costs of fuel and

purchased power are properly allocated on an energy basis because they vary with energy

production, PTC benefits should be allocated on an energy basis because they are earned as a

function of energy production. A class that consumes more energy causes a greater need for

generation, which in turn generates more PTCs.                       That class should therefore receive a

proportionally larger share of the PTC benefit.

          The Certification’s principal rationale for departing from the Stipulation’s energy

allocation is that PTC benefits should follow the allocation of the costs of the resources that

generate them, illustrated by an analogy to two investors in a print shop. 32 OPL respectfully

submits that the analogy does not fit utility ratemaking. The fixed costs of SPS’s production plant,

including the PTC-generating resources, are recovered in base rates and allocated among classes

using AED-4CP, so each class’s relative contribution to the cost of those facilities is therefore

already recognized, in full, through the base-rate allocation. 33 But PTCs are not a return of the

capital customers contributed; they are a production-based tax credit that is passed through the

energy-based FPPCAC. Matching that energy-based benefit to the energy that each class causes

SPS to generate is consistent with cost-causation.

         Moreover, the AED-4CP allocator is not a better fit for allocating PTC benefits. AED-4CP

is itself energy-weighted: the average-demand component represents each class’s share of energy

use. 34 The remainder is the excess-demand component, which measures each class’s contribution

to SPS’s summer peak capacity requirements. 35 But nothing about the PTC calculation depends

on a class’s contribution to peak demand, and contrary to the Certification’s assumption, the

excess-demand component of the AED-4CP does not necessarily reflect each class’s contributions

to funding the renewable generators that create PTCs because peak demand generally drives

investment in dispatchable resources such as thermal generation or batteries.

              Certification at ¶¶ 177–180, 184.

fixed costs of the renewable resources are allocated based on the combination of average energy demands and the
additional capacity needed for reliability).

        The Certification also observes that fuel prices are the same for all classes, whereas the

costs of the renewable resources are not. 36 But differences in classes’ responsibility for the fixed

costs of renewable plant are a function of the base-rate demand allocation already discussed, and

do not change the fact that each kWh of renewable generation earns the same credit regardless of

which class consumes it. The Hearing Examiners’ alternative suggestion—to calculate each class’s

“actual monetary contribution” to energy production using the energy-cost component embedded

in each class’s rates—should also not be adopted because it was not proposed by any party, was

not developed in the record, and was not adopted in the Certification. 37

                  2.       The stipulated PTC allocation preserves SPS’s existing practice and
                           avoids complicating SPS’s FPPCAC and related true-ups.

       SPS already credits the PTCs generated by its Hale and Sagamore wind facilities through

its FPPCAC on an energy basis. 38 The FPPCAC is structured as an energy-based charge recovered

on a dollar-per-kWh basis, and all costs and credits currently included in the FPPCAC are allocated

among classes on an energy basis. 39 The Commission has approved crediting the solar PTCs to

customers through the FPPCAC, and the Stipulation (and the Certification) continue that

treatment. 40 As SPS explained, the energy allocation “preserves SPS’s existing FPPCAC

allocation practice and avoids creating a second allocation and true-up process for the new solar

PTCs.” 41 By contrast, the AED-4CP approach would require SPS to apply forecasted demand

 allocators within the fuel clause and true them up to actuals annually. 42 Introducing a demand-

based allocation into an otherwise energy-based mechanism would be a departure from current

practice, and the Certification does not address the administrative consequences of that departure.

                    3.      Even if the Commission adopts the Certification’s position on PTC
                            allocation, it should not apply that change retroactively to Hale and
                            Sagamore PTCs.

        OPL notes that the Certification could be read such that an AED-4CP allocation would

apply to all of SPS’s PTCs, and not just the PTCs from SPS’s new solar facilities. However, no

party in this case ever proposed changing the longstanding energy allocation that SPS has used for

PTCs generated by its Hale and Sagamore wind facilities, and the Stipulation was not intended to

impact the allocation of those PTCs. Accordingly, in the event the Commission adopts the

Certification’s position on PTC allocation, which it should not, OPL urges the Commission to

clarify in its final order that the AED-4CP allocation only applies to PTCs generated by SPS’s new

solar facilities.

IV.     CONCLUSION

        For the reasons discussed above, the Commission should approve the Stipulation as

written, without the modifications proposed by the Hearings Examiners.
